images.title: Longer boundary, smaller area
images.purpose: Shows a rectangle with a larger perimeter but a smaller area than another.
images.composition: Two rectangles side by side on the same baseline, both drawn on 1 cm unit squares at the same scale.
images.exact_structure: Plain white background, lots of empty space, the figure large and centred, thin dark outlines. Only the labels listed appear; no other text, no scenery, no characters. LEFT: a strip 10 squares long and 1 square tall, 10 unit squares, filled teal (#0072B2), each unit square outlined thinly. Label 10 cm under the long side and 1 cm beside the short side. RIGHT: a rectangle 5 squares long and 4 squares tall, 20 unit squares in 4 rows of 5, filled amber (#E69F00), each unit square outlined thinly. Label 5 cm under it and 4 cm beside it. The outer boundary of each shape is traced with a thick reddish purple (#CC79A7) line. Under the strip, two short lines: Perimeter 22 cm and Area 10 cm². Under the rectangle: Perimeter 18 cm and Area 20 cm². Check: 2 × (10 + 1) = 22, 10 × 1 = 10, 2 × (5 + 4) = 18, 5 × 4 = 20.
rejection: any count of objects, cells, ticks or rows that differs from the numbers stated in the spec
any text beyond the listed visible text, or any listed text misspelled or altered
any board name, publisher name, book title, page number or curriculum branding anywhere in the frame
a hyphen used in place of a minus sign on any labelled number
images.takeaway: The strip has the longer boundary but holds only half as many squares.
images.description: Shows a rectangle with a larger perimeter but a smaller area than another.
images.context: Uses the concept's own example: 10 by 1 strip against 5 by 4 rectangle.
images.teaching_notes: Point at the thick boundary for perimeter and the filled squares for area.

image_decisions.why: The misconception that perimeter measures area is broken by one countable side by side pair.
